title: Interfaces and Abstract Classes
summary: Abstract classes and abstract methods, interfaces as contracts, implementing several interfaces, default and static interface methods, programming to an interface, the built-in Comparable and Iterable, functional interfaces as a preview of lambdas, and choosing between an interface and an abstract class.

cards.q: Can you create an object of an abstract class with `new`?
cards.a:
No; only of concrete subclasses that implement every abstract method

`new Shape(...)` does not compile when `Shape` is abstract. An abstract class can still have constructors, which its subclasses call with `super(...)`.

cards.q: Why must a method that implements an interface method be `public`?
cards.a:
Interface methods are implicitly public, and an implementation may not reduce visibility

Leaving out `public` gives the method package access, which is narrower than the interface's public method, so the compiler refuses it.

cards.q: A class wants to be sortable with `Collections.sort`. What should it implement?
cards.a:
`Comparable<T>`

`Comparable` defines the natural order through `compareTo`, which `Collections.sort` uses. `Iterable` only makes it usable in an enhanced for.
